{{Short description|Phenomenon of fluid mechanics}}
{{Distinguish|Kelvin–Helmholtz mechanism}}
{{More footnotes|date=March 2010}}

[[File:Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability.ogv|thumb|right|Numerical simulation of a temporal Kelvin–Helmholtz instability]]
The '''Kelvin–Helmholtz instability''' (after [[Lord Kelvin]] and [[Hermann von Helmholtz]]) is a [[fluid instability]] that occurs when there is [[shear velocity|velocity shear]] in a single [[continuum mechanics|continuous fluid]] or a velocity difference across the interface between two [[fluid]]s. Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities are visible in the [[atmosphere]]s of planets and moons, such as in [[List of cloud types|cloud formations]] on [[Earth]] or the [[Great Red Spot#Great Red Spot|Red Spot]] on [[Jupiter]], and the [[Sun#Atmosphere|atmosphere of the Sun]].<ref name=":0">{{cite web|last=Fox|first=Karen C.|title=NASA's Solar Dynamics Observatory Catches "Surfer" Waves on the Sun|url=http://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/sunearth/news/sun-surfing.html|website=NASA-The Sun-Earth Connection: Heliophysics|date=30 December 2014|publisher=NASA|access-date=21 July 2011|archive-date=20 November 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211120110428/https://www.nasa.gov/mission_pages/sunearth/news/sun-surfing.html}}</ref>
[[File:Spatial KH 2D vorticity.gif|thumb|Spatially developing 2D Kelvin-Helmholtz instability at low [[Reynolds number]]. Small perturbations, imposed at the inlet on the tangential velocity, evolve in the computational box. High Reynolds number would be marked with an increase of small scale motions.]]

==Theory overview and mathematical concepts==
[[File:Wavecloudsduval.jpg|thumb|left|A KH instability rendered visible by clouds, known as fluctus,<ref>{{cite news|last1=Sutherland|first1=Scott|title=Cloud Atlas joins the digital age while adding a dozen new cloud types|url=https://www.theweathernetwork.com/en/news/science/earth-science/international-cloud-atlas-digital-update-adds-11-new-cloud-types|access-date=13 August 2025|work=The Weather Network|agency=Pelmorex Media|date=March 23, 2017}}</ref> over [[Mount Duval (New South Wales)|Mount Duval]] in Australia|200x200px]]
[[File:Saturn Kelvin Helmholtz.jpg|thumb|right|A KH instability on the planet Saturn, formed at the interaction of two bands of the planet's atmosphere|200x200px]]
[[File:Deep Oceanic Kelvin-Helmholtz billows.jpg|thumb|left|Kelvin-Helmholtz billows 500m deep in the Atlantic Ocean|200x200px]]
[[File:Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability.gif|thumb|Animation of the KH instability, using a second order 2D finite volume scheme|200x200px]]
[[File:Kelvin Helmholtz cloud formation during Hartford sunset.jpg|thumb|left|Kelvin-Helmholtz cloud formation over [[Hartford, Connecticut]]|200x200px]]
[[File:Kelvin-Helmholtz_instability_in_the_sun's_atmosphere_on_April_8,_2010.jpg|thumb|KH instability in the Sun's atmosphere|200x200px]]
[[Fluid dynamics]] predicts the onset of instability and transition to [[turbulent flow]] within [[fluid]]s of different [[density|densities]] moving at different speeds.<ref name="Drazin">{{cite book |last1=Drazin |first1=P. G.|year=2003 |title=Encyclopedia of Atmospheric Sciences |publisher=Elsevier Ltd. |pages=1068–1072 |doi=10.1016/B978-0-12-382225-3.00190-0 }}</ref> If surface tension is ignored, two fluids in parallel motion with different velocities and densities yield an interface that is unstable to short-wavelength perturbations for all speeds. However, [[surface tension]] is able to stabilize the short wavelength instability up to a threshold velocity.

Suppose we have two parallel plane streams of fluid of same density with speeds <math>U_1</math> and <math>U_2</math>. Then the perturbed interface with the normal-mode decomposition <math>e^{i(kx-\omega t)}</math> obeys the dispersion relation (for ideal flow with no surface tension),

:<math>\omega = k \frac{\rho_1 U_1 + \rho_2 U_2}{\rho_1+\rho_2} + i \frac{i\sqrt{\rho_1\rho_2}}{\rho_1+\rho_2}|U_1-U_2|</math>.

If the density and velocity vary continuously in space (with the lighter layers uppermost, so that the fluid is [[Rayleigh–Taylor instability|RT-stable]]), the dynamics of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability is described by the [[Taylor–Goldstein equation]]: 
<math display="block">(U-c)^2\left({d^2\tilde\phi \over d z^2} - k^2\tilde\phi\right) +\left[N^2-(U-c){d^2 U \over d z^2}\right]\tilde\phi = 0,</math> where <math display="inline">N = \sqrt{g / L_\rho}</math> denotes the [[Brunt–Väisälä frequency]], U is the horizontal parallel velocity, k is the wave number, c is the eigenvalue parameter of the problem, <math>\tilde\phi</math> is complex amplitude of the [[stream function]]. Its onset is given by the [[Richardson number]] <math>\mathrm{Ri}</math>. Typically the layer is unstable for <math>\mathrm{Ri} < 0.25</math>. These effects are common in cloud layers. The study of this instability is applicable in plasma physics, for example in [[inertial confinement fusion]] and the [[Plasma (physics)|plasma]]–[[beryllium]] interface. In situations where there is a state of static stability (where there is a continuous density gradient), the [[Rayleigh–Taylor instability]] is often insignificant compared to the magnitude of the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability.

Numerically, the Kelvin–Helmholtz instability is simulated in a temporal or a spatial approach. In the temporal approach, the flow is considered in a periodic (cyclic) box "moving" at mean speed (absolute instability). In the spatial approach, simulations mimic a lab experiment with natural inlet and outlet conditions (convective instability).


== Discovery and history==

The existence of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability was first discovered by German physiologist and physicist Hermann von Helmholtz in 1868. Helmholtz identified that "every perfect geometrically sharp edge by which a fluid flows must tear it asunder and establish a surface of separation".<ref>{{cite journal |title=XLIII. On discontinuous movements of fluids |journal=The London, Edinburgh, and Dublin Philosophical Magazine and Journal of Science |date=1 November 1868 |volume=36 |issue=244 |pages=337–346 |doi=10.1080/14786446808640073 |last1=von Helmholtz |first=Hermann}}</ref><ref name="Drazin"></ref> Following that work, in 1871, collaborator [[William Thomson, 1st Baron Kelvin|William Thomson]] (later Lord Kelvin), developed a mathematical solution of linear instability whilst attempting to model the formation of ocean wind waves.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Matsuoka |first=Chihiro |date=2014-03-31 |title=Kelvin-Helmholtz Instability and Roll-up |journal=Scholarpedia |language=en |volume=9 |issue=3 |article-number=11821 |doi=10.4249/scholarpedia.11821 |bibcode=2014SchpJ...911821M |issn=1941-6016|doi-access=free }}</ref>

Throughout the early 20th Century, the ideas of Kelvin-Helmholtz instabilities were applied to a range of stratified fluid applications. In the early 1920s, [[Lewis Fry Richardson]] developed the concept that such shear instability would only form where shear overcame static stability due to stratification, encapsulated in the [[Richardson Number]]. 

Geophysical observations of the Kelvin-Helmholtz instability were made through the late 1960s/early 1970s, for clouds,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ludlam |first1=F. H. |title=Characteristics of billow clouds and their relation to clear-air turbulence |journal=Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society |date=October 1967 |volume=93 |issue=398 |pages=419–435 |doi=10.1002/qj.49709339803|bibcode=1967QJRMS..93..419L }}</ref> and later the ocean.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Woods |first1=J. D. |title=Wave-induced shear instability in the summer thermocline |journal=Journal of Fluid Mechanics |date=18 June 1968 |volume=32 |issue=4 |pages=791–800 |doi=10.1017/S0022112068001035|bibcode=1968JFM....32..791W |s2cid=67827521 }}</ref>


== Kelvin–Helmholtz instability in compressible flows: Landau stabilization ==

The Kelvin–Helmholtz instability in compressible flows was first studied by [[Lev Landau]] in 1944,<ref>Landau, L. (1944). Stability of tangential discontinuities in compressible fluid. In Dokl. Akad. Nauk SSSR (Vol. 44, No. 4, pp. 151-153).</ref> and was later refined by Sergei Ivanovich Syrovatskii in 1954.<ref>Syrovatskii, S. I. (1954). INSTABILITY OF TANGENTIAL DISCONTINUITIES IN A COMPRESSIBLE MEDIUM.</ref> Suppose <math>U_2=0</math> and <math>U_1=U</math> (which can always be achieved by a suitable choice of the frame of reference); then the dispersion relation for the normal mode <math>e^{i(k_xx+k_yy-\omega t)}</math> is given by

:<math>\left[\frac{1}{\omega^2}-\frac{1}{(\omega-Uk_x)^2}\right]\left[\frac{1}{c^2k^2}-\frac{1}{\omega^2}-\frac{1}{(\omega-Uk_x)^2}\right]=0, \qquad k = \sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2}</math>,

where <math>c</math> is the [[sound speed]]. The zero of the first factor is <math>\omega=\tfrac{1}{2}Uk_x</math>, which is always real. The zeros of the second factor are given by solving the bi-quadratic form in terms of <math>(\omega - \tfrac{1}{2}Uk_x)</math>:

:<math>\omega = \tfrac{1}{2}Uk_x \pm \sqrt{\frac{1}{4}U^2k_x^2 + c^2k^2 \pm c^2k^2\sqrt{1 + \frac{U^2k_x^2}{c^2k^2}}}.</math>

These roots are real only if <math>Uk_x/ck>2\sqrt{2}\approx 2.83</math>, as shown elegantly by Landau. Let <math>\phi</math> be the angle between the velocity flow <math>U\mathbf{e}_x</math> and the wavevector <math>\mathbf{k}=k_x\mathbf{e}_x+k_y\mathbf{e}_y</math>. Since <math>k_x = k \cos\phi</math>, the instability condition can be rewritten as

:<math>M \cos\phi < 2\sqrt{2}, \quad M=\frac{U}{c};</math>

here <math>M</math> is the [[Mach number]]. The above condition yields two distinct physical regimes based on the Mach number of the flow:<ref>Gerwin, R. A. (1968). Stability of the interface between two fluids in relative motion. Reviews of Modern Physics, 40(3), 652.</ref>
* If the flow velocity is relatively low, specifically <math>M < 2\sqrt{2}</math>, the inequality holds for all angles, meaning the flow is unstable to perturbations propagating in any direction along the interface.
* If the flow is highly supersonic such that <math>M \ge 2\sqrt{2}</math>, the interface becomes completely stabilized against directional perturbations traveling within a forward cone where <math>\cos\phi \ge 2\sqrt{2}/M</math>; this is known as the '''Landau stabilization'''. In this supersonic regime, the instability only appears for oblique waves propagating at sufficiently large angles relative to the flow, satisfying <math>\cos\phi < 2\sqrt{2}/M.</math>

Landau in his original 1944 paper considered only the case where <math>\phi=0</math> (i.e., <math>k_y=0</math>), leading to the prediction that the interface becomes completely stable at high supersonic speeds. However, [[Yakov Zeldovich]] subsequently conducted a laboratory experiment testing this phenomenon and found that the interface remains highly unstable and transitions into turbulence. Sergei I. Syrovatskii's 1954 generalization for arbitrary values of <math>\phi</math> provided the missing mathematical framework, proving that oblique waves (<math>k_y \neq 0</math>) will always grow, thereby explaining the experimental instability observed by Zeldovich.
